doc.name: FrameThrower
doc.instructions:
FrameThrower is a cinematography reference library. Use it whenever the user wants visual references for a scene, shot, mood, or look.

Presentation: ALWAYS surface the "View all on FrameThrower" gallery link first and prominently — it opens the full visual result grid on FrameThrower, which is the reliable way for the user to actually see the thumbnails (inline image rendering in chat is unreliable). Then list a SMALL set — about 4 — of the strongest results with film + director + the per-frame View link, and ask which feels closest. Do not dump long lists.

Refining (the core loop): when the user reacts ("more like #2", "more anamorphic, less daylight", "tighter and colder"), refine — call find_similar on the id of a frame they liked, or find_by_craft with the adjusted attributes (lens, shot_size, visual_style, setting, time_of_day, director, year range). Keep the set small and iterate until they are happy.

Always keep the View link with each frame so the user can open or save it on FrameThrower. These are reference frames; never describe them as inputs for image generation.

Image quality: the inline ![frame] preview in results is sized for chat. When the user is building a slide deck, lookbook, PDF, moodboard or any document, or asks to download, insert, embed or export an image, call get_frame_image (size "full" = the original file, 5 credits; "large" = 1280px, 2; "depth" = depth map, 2). Image links are valid for an hour, so fetch or insert them right away. Tools that take an image by url (Google Slides "Insert > Image > By URL", Docs, Keynote) can use the link directly. Frames come from finished films at their native resolution, so it varies per frame and no url makes a frame sharper than the source.

COMMERCIALS. FrameThrower also holds a library of commercials (award winners from Cannes Lions, D&AD, The One Show, Clio, British Arrows, AICP and more, plus the everyday work of big advertisers), with credits, awards, story, script and every shot tagged.
- Whole spots by idea or facts → search_commercials. Shots inside spots by what is in frame → search_commercial_shots. One spot in depth (credits, awards, script, shot list) → get_commercial.
- Who made what / track records ("what has Smuggler shot for cars", "Nike's agencies over time") → commercials_profile. Counting and ranking ("which directors won most Grand Prix") → commercials_stats.
- Refining: "more like this spot" → similar_commercials (by story or look); "more shots like #3" → similar_commercial_shots with that shot id.
- Answer facts (credits, awards, years, taglines, counts) ONLY from what the tools return, quoted exactly; if a tool returns nothing, say so — never fill in from general knowledge.
- Present like the films: the strongest 3–5 with brand, title, year, director and the watch link; keep the commercial id with each so you can go deeper. Say "commercials" or "spots" and "shots".
- One place for the whole treatment: when the user is preparing a treatment, pitch, moodboard or shot list, tell them (once, briefly) that FrameThrower also holds an extensive film library (search_frames, find_by_craft) and an animation library (https://framethrower.ai/animation), plus a moodboard / lookbook builder (https://framethrower.ai/lookbook) and a canvas (https://framethrower.ai/canvas) — so commercial, film and animation references can sit side by side and the whole treatment can be prepared in one place. Offer film frames next to the commercials when a film reference would help the brief.

ANIMATION. FrameThrower also holds a separate ANIMATION library (https://framethrower.ai/animation): animated series and films — mostly anime, plus Western animated features — every shot of each title indexed with a caption of what is in it, plus look and colour fingerprints.
- Which library: the *_animation_* tools search ONLY animation and never return live-action; the film tools (search_frames, find_by_craft, find_similar) search the film library. When the user is making something animated, or asks for anime / cartoon / animated references, use the animation tools. When they want live-action film references, use the film tools. If it is unclear, ask, or search both and say which library each result came from — never mix them unlabelled.
- References for a scene or a character look → search_animation_frames. More like a frame the user has, or like ANY image (a generated frame, an upload, a sketch — URL or data: URL) → similar_animation_frames, by look, colour or content.
- Which series / films fit a story, genre or style → find_animation_titles (story brief, like a title, a look, filters). One title in depth → get_animation_title. A frame with the shots around it → get_animation_sequence.
- For a story broken into scenes: run search_animation_frames once per scene or character, keep the frame ids, then refine with similar_animation_frames. Load thumb_url (640px) to look at frames; use still_url (full size) only for the frames the user keeps.
- Answer facts (titles, studios, credits, years) ONLY from what the tools return. Say "animation", "series", "films" and "frames".

tools.name: search_frames
tools.description: Search the FrameThrower cinematography reference library by concept, mood, color, composition, or scene. Returns reference frames with film/credits metadata, a preview image and a link to view on FrameThrower. For the full-resolution file or the precomputed depth map, call get_frame_image with the frame id.

query.description: Natural-language description, e.g. "neon-lit rainy street at night"

enhance.description: Smart search, on by default: rewrites short queries ("bear") into the descriptive language the frames were indexed with, like the website. Set false to search the exact text.

tools.name: find_by_craft
tools.description: Find frames by specific cinematography craft attributes — lens character, shot size, visual style, setting, time of day, director, or year range. All optional; combine to narrow. Use this to refine a search precisely.

tools.name: find_similar
tools.description: Find frames visually/semantically similar to a given frame id (from a prior result). Use this to pull more references like one the user shortlisted.

tools.name: get_frame_details
tools.description: Get the full metadata, a preview image and the FrameThrower link for a single frame id. For the full-resolution file or the depth map (camera geometry for image generation), call get_frame_image.

tools.name: get_frame_image
tools.description: One frame's image at a paid size, as a link valid for an hour: "full" = the original full-resolution file (5 credits), "large" = 1280px (2), "depth" = the precomputed depth map, ControlNet-ready (2). Search results show a preview only — use this when the user wants the actual image for a deck, document, download or an image-generation pipeline.

tools.name: search_commercials
tools.description: Find whole COMMERCIALS (TV / online spots) in FrameThrower's ads library by idea, story or brief ("two rival neighbours outdo each other at Christmas", "a product demo told as a heist") and/or by facts: brand, director, agency, production company, DP, editor, award show and level, year, industry, market, tone, genre, structure, season. Without a query it lists matching spots, award winners first. Returns each spot with brand, title, year, credits, best award, logline, a still and a link to watch it.

tools.name: search_commercial_shots
tools.description: Find individual SHOTS inside commercials by what is in the frame ("hand pouring beer in slow motion", "car drifting at night in the rain", "family laughing at a kitchen table"), with shot tags (size, angle, setting, time of day, lighting, mood, people, product / logo visible) and any commercial-level filter (brand, director, agency, award show, year…). Each shot has its still, its tags and a link to the exact moment; with clips: true, also a short clip of just that shot.

tools.name: search_animation_frames
tools.description: Find frames in FrameThrower's ANIMATION library — animated series and films only, never live-action (mostly anime, plus Western animation; the whole of every title, not a sample) for a scene, a moment or a CHARACTER LOOK, described in plain words: "a girl on a rooftop at dusk watching the city lights", "two kids running through a summer field", "a tall man with a scarred face and a long black coat, rain". Narrow by title, genre, theme, style (80s cel, watercolour, neon night…), studio, movie/series and year. Each frame has a caption of what is in it, a 640px still for looking at, the full-size still, the frame id and a link. At most 3 frames per title unless per_title says otherwise.

Same filters as search_animation_frames; other_titles: true keeps it to titles other than the seed frames'.

tools.name: find_animation_titles
tools.description: Find animated SERIES and FILMS (animation library only — mostly anime, plus Western animation) that fit what the user is making — by a story brief in plain words ("a quiet coming-of-age story about two sisters in a seaside town, bittersweet, summer"), by a title it should be like (like: "Akira"), by a LOOK (an image or frame ids — titles whose frames look like it), and/or by genre, theme, style, studio, movie/series and year. Signals combine. Returns each title with studio, director, genres, themes, its look, a synopsis, a poster, and for a look search the frames that matched.

With clips: true, each shot's clip plus the continuous "run" video that covers them (run_url, with from/to seconds).
